## Overview

The Ludza Estonians—Estonian: *lutsi maarahvas*, “Lutsi country folk”; Latvian: *ludzas igauņi*—are a South Estonian-speaking community of Latgale in south-eastern Latvia. Before World War II, they lived in about 53 villages across the rural parishes of Pilda, Nirza, Brigi, and Mērdzene, all surrounding the town of Ludza. Their language, the Lutsi dialect, belongs to the same family as Võro and Seto and developed in isolation for several centuries. Oskar Kallas counted 4,387 inhabitants identified as ethnic Lutsi in 1893, of whom approximately 800 still spoke the dialect. The community later collapsed as a Lutsi-speaking society: the dialect ceased to be used for daily interaction during the 1970s and 1980s, and no remaining speakers were identified by 2021. The group matters to folk-culture research because its language, Catholic parish life, migration history, and long isolation preserve evidence of a South Estonian cultural island in Latgale.

## Festivals & rituals

They do document Roman Catholic affiliation and state that Catholic services and confession were conducted in Lutsi during the period when the community remained culturally distinct and largely confined to its home parishes. This information does not specify particular feast days, ritual forms, or life-cycle practices.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources document substantial linguistic and folkloristic work. Sustained documentation of Lutsi began with the 1893 expedition of the Estonian folklorist and linguist Oskar Kallas, whose material was published the following year as *Lutsi maarahvas*. The sources also mention pre-war fieldwork by Paulopriit Voolaine and August Sang’s 1936 surveys. Since the 2010s, documentation and revitalisation funded between 2013 and 2016 by the Kone Foundation have produced a Lutsi primer, *Lutsi kiele lementar*, a beginner’s grammar reference, and a dictionary.

## Language & religion

Lutsi is a South Estonian language island most closely related to Seto within the Võro–Seto branch. Several centuries of contact with Latvian, especially the local Latgalian dialect, Russian, and Polish produced loanwords and phonological and morphological influence. By the 19th century, Russian had become the dominant language of administration and inter-ethnic communication. Polish was heard mainly on the manors because it had been the administrative language of Polish Livonia.

Unlike most Estonian speakers, the Lutsi were Roman Catholic, in keeping with the Catholic tradition of Latgale under the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, to which Polish Livonia belonged until 1772. Catholic services and confession were conducted in Lutsi until parish life was Latvianised. By 2013, surveys identified one partial speaker and several rememberers; by 2021, no remaining speakers were identified. The last person commonly identified as a fluent speaker was Nikolājs Nikonovs (1944–2006), from Lielie Tjapši, called *Jānikülǟ* in Lutsi, in Pilda parish. His wife Antonīna Nikonova (1949–2014) was the last person with substantial passive knowledge of the dialect.
